extracted.intended_audience: immigration practitioners, DHS adjudicators, policymakers, and public commenters on the public-charge rule
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and interpretation of the INA public-charge inadmissibility provision and the DHS regulatory implementation (which benefits are considered, relevant definitions, procedural timing, and interpretive approach). Applicable to adjudications, visa/adjustment determinations, and rulemaking commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory public-charge inadmissibility standard (INA 212(a)(4)(A))
rubrics_metrics.description: “Any alien, who in the opinion of the consular officer at the time of application for a visa, or in the opinion of the Attorney General at the time of the application for admission or adjustment of status, is likely at any time to become a public charge is inadmissible.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a subjective, opinion-based statutory standard that delegates determination to consular officers or the Attorney General (or their delegates). Cited authorities (e.g., Matter of Harutunian; Matter of Martinez-Lopez) emphasize the subjective/delegated nature of the determination and that such borderline determinations are generally beyond the reach of judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive approach: degree of dependence, not scale of expenditures
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS believes the term “public charge” is best interpreted by reference to the degree of an individual's dependence on the government for support, rather than the scale of overall government expenditures for particular programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although DHS acknowledges that non-cash benefits involve significant government expenditures and are prevalent, the Department emphasizes assessing whether an individual is dependent on public support. The preamble cites DHS's prior statements (e.g., 2018 NPRM) and explains that DHS limits consideration of past receipt to the benefits covered by this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited consideration of past receipt to specified benefits covered by the rule
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS limits consideration of past receipt of public benefits to the benefits covered by this rule (examples used in analysis: individual's Medicaid or SSI participation and the family's SNAP, housing, TANF, or General Assistance participation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical analyses referenced (e.g., CPS analysis) focus on six forms of assistance covered by the 2019 Final Rule. DHS explains that receipt of noncash benefits is more prevalent and that it has limited past-receipt consideration to the enumerated benefits for reasons stated throughout the preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replacement/definition of institutionalization term
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of the rule, DHS is replacing the term “institutionalization for long-term care at government expense” with the term “long-term institutionalization.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a definitional change in wording adopted for the regulatory text; the preamble notes the replacement explicitly (contrasting prior NPRM/Field Guidance phrasing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing-eligibility requirement at time of filing through adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant or petitioner must establish that they are eligible for the requested benefit at the time of filing the benefit request and must continue to be eligible through adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 8 CFR 103.2(b)(1) and Matter of Alarcon (20 I&N Dec. 557, 562) which explain that admissibility is determined based on the facts and law at the time the application is finally considered; applications are ‘continuing’.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between inadmissibility (public charge) and removability assessments
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of removability for public charge is different from the assessment of public-charge inadmissibility and is not part of this rule, though USCIS may assess whether an applicant was properly admitted for naturalization purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites INA sec. 237(a)(5) and INA sec. 318 and explains that USCIS may consider past admissibility in naturalization adjudications, but removability procedures/standards are separate and outside the scope of this rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive meaning of 'public charge' as dependency (judicial precedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Court decisions have construed 'public charge' historically as meaning dependency — being a persistent 'charge' on the public purse — and held that mere receipt of benefits does not necessarily constitute such dependency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites New York v. DHS, City & County of San Francisco v. USCIS, Cook County v. Wolf, Casa de Maryland v. Trump, and related decisions discussing historical meanings and concluding that the settled meaning centers on dependence; courts also recognize the executive's delegated discretion in defining and implementing the term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of statutory modifier 'primarily'
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'primarily' can mean 'first,' 'chief,' or 'principal' but can also mean 'essentially,' 'fundamentally,' or 'substantially.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Board of Governors v. Agnew and Malat v. Riddell for canon/precedent about the range of meanings for 'primarily' when interpreting statutory text; useful when construing provisions using that modifier in this regulatory context (e.g., primary dependence).
